profiles.meeting_scenario: A pediatric hospitalist service is preparing to standardize family-centered rounds (FCRs) on a 28-bed general pediatrics unit before the July trainee turnover. This coordination meeting is between the physician leading the FCR rollout and the nurse manager responsible for unit operations. They need to align on the daily rounding workflow, what each side will prepare before rounds, how bedside nurses will be incorporated, which patients should be discussed outside the room first, and how the team's daily plan and follow-up items will be captured. The agenda is to confirm the 8:30 start, identify the shared patient list for pre-round updates, define bedside-versus-hallway exceptions for sensitive patients, and agree on where the daily plan/action items will be documented during the pilot. The expected outcome is an apparently shared launch plan for next Monday with no obvious open disagreements.

members.name: Dr. Maya Chen
members.role: Pediatric Hospitalist and FCR Implementation Lead
members.expertise: Inpatient pediatrics, resident education, bedside communication, quality improvement
members.background: Dr. Chen is a hospitalist who completed a QI fellowship and recently joined the hospital's patient experience committee; she previously trained at a larger children's hospital where structured family-centered rounds were routine and is now adapting that model locally.
members.private_state: She wants a clean early rollout that attendings and residents will actually follow, and she is wary of adding operational steps that make rounds feel slower or duplicative from the physician team's perspective.
hidden_assumptions: If rounds 'start at 8:30,' the attending-led team should be entering the first patient's room at 8:30 rather than gathering then.
The 'shared list' naturally refers to the resident-maintained EHR physician census/handoff list, because that is the list the medical team updates in real time.
A 'sensitive patient' exception should be narrow and reserved for unusually delicate situations like suspected abuse, major family conflict, or imminent bad-news discussions.
Saying the team will 'document the daily plan' or 'track action items' means the resident's daily progress note and task sign-out in the EHR, since that is the formal clinical record.
If key next steps are verbalized clearly during bedside rounds, duplicating them in a separate unit tool is optional during the pilot.

members.name: Elena Ruiz, RN, MSN
members.expertise: Inpatient nursing operations, staffing workflow, safety huddles, discharge coordination
members.background: Ruiz has managed the pediatric unit for five years and previously served as charge nurse; she is highly attuned to how morning med pass, interpreter coordination, isolation logistics, and discharge teaching affect whether a new rounding process will stick on the floor.
members.private_state: She wants FCRs to be workable for bedside nurses without creating hidden interruptions, and she wants any commitments made on rounds captured in the same operational workflow nurses already rely on during the shift.
hidden_assumptions: If rounds 'start at 8:30,' that means the team convenes at 8:30 and begins room entry only after the charge nurse helps line up bedside nurses and checks immediate med-pass conflicts.

The 'shared list' refers to the unit's printed interdisciplinary list annotated by charge nurse and case management, because that is what coordinates nursing, discharge, interpreter, and isolation workflow.

A 'sensitive patient' category routinely includes adolescents with confidential history, social work or CPS concerns, behavioral escalation, or any family likely to need an initial hallway framing conversation.

When people say they will 'document the daily plan' or 'track action items,' that implies using the unit's rounding tracker and bedside whiteboard so nurses can see and act on follow-up items in real time.
If a plan is only in the physician note, it has not really been operationally captured for the bedside team during that shift.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to start rounds at 8:30
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that rounds will 'start at 8:30.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the attending, residents, and students should be walking into the first patient's room at 8:30.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the group begins gathering and coordinating at 8:30, with first room entry a few minutes later after nurses are located and immediate workflow conflicts are checked.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds exact and routine, so it feels like a settled scheduling anchor rather than something needing unpacking; each person assumes the other uses the same default hospital meaning.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss updating and using 'the shared list' before rounds.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the EHR-based physician census/handoff list that residents already maintain and can update before the team starts.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the unit's printed interdisciplinary list marked by charge nurse with interpreter needs, isolation precautions, likely discharges, and logistical flags.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both lists are genuinely shared across disciplines in different ways, and each is the obvious default in the speaker's workflow, so the noun phrase feels fully specific without either person naming the artifact.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that 'sensitive patients' may need an outside-the-room discussion first.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this exception is a narrow carve-out for unusually delicate circumstances such as suspected non-accidental trauma, custody disputes, or preparing to deliver major bad news.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the category is broader and routinely includes adolescent confidentiality issues, pending CPS or social work concerns, behavioral incidents, or families the nurse expects will need initial framing before bedside discussion.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They share the same values of privacy and flow, so the label 'sensitive' creates immediate cooperative agreement while hiding different boundaries for which patients are actually included.

misalignment_points.topic: Where the daily plan and follow-up items will be captured
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that the team will 'document the daily plan' and 'track action items' from FCRs.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the resident will capture the plan in the daily progress note and, when needed, in the physician team's EHR sign-out/task workflow.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means action items will be entered into the unit's standard rounding tracker and reflected on the bedside whiteboard so nurses can use them during the shift.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They are aligned on the need to capture follow-up, and each assumes there is one obvious institutional way to do that; because both methods are normal and not framed as competing systems, the conversation never pauses on the implementation details.

turns.inner_thought: I need this pilot locked in for Monday without adding a bunch of extra operational layers that will bog down the team. If we can agree that the resident updates the EHR physician census/handoff list ahead of time and captures the plan in the usual note and sign-out workflow, this will feel familiar enough that attendings and residents will actually do it.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time, Elena. I'd like to have the FCR pilot ready to launch next Monday, so I was hoping today we could confirm timing, how bedside nurses will join in, what we'll use as the shared list, and how we'll document the daily plan and track action items during rounds.

turns.inner_thought: Nursing will support this if it fits real unit flow. 'Start at 8:30' needs to mean we convene then, not that a giant team is suddenly at the first door while nurses are in med pass or unavailable. I need enough room for charge to line people up and avoid immediate workflow collisions.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. The nurses are very supportive of trying this. I mainly want to make sure rounds start at 8:30 in a way that lets us pull bedside nurses in without creating problems right in the busiest part of the morning.

turns.inner_thought: Good, we're aligned on 8:30. If the senior resident updates the EHR shared list before then, the attending-led team can walk into the first room right at 8:30 and keep moving. I don't want a pre-round staging step that shifts actual bedside time later.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. The senior resident can update the shared list before rounds, and that should help us start at 8:30 and move room to room pretty efficiently.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. Charge can prep the printed interdisciplinary list before the team gathers at 8:30, with interpreter needs, isolation, and discharge priorities marked so we know how to sequence things and which nurses we need to grab.
turns.utterance: Great. On our side, the charge nurse can make sure the shared list has interpreter needs, isolation flags, and expected discharges marked before rounds begin.

turns.inner_thought: I want bedside rounds to be the norm, with only a small carve-out for truly delicate cases like suspected abuse, major family conflict, or a bad-news setup. If the exception list gets too broad, we'll end up back in hallway rounds by default.
turns.utterance: For the actual workflow, I'd like bedside FCR to be the default for essentially every patient, with just a few sensitive patients getting a brief outside-the-room discussion first.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, and nurses should be able to flag the adolescents with confidentiality issues, the social work or CPS concerns, behavioral situations, and families who need framing before the team enters. That's exactly where an outside conversation keeps things smoother and safer.
turns.utterance: I think that's very workable. The bedside nurses can flag sensitive patients ahead of time so the team knows which rooms may need an outside conversation before going in.

turns.inner_thought: The resident needs to close each encounter with a crisp plan and put it straight into the progress note and task workflow as we go. If we do that in real time, we avoid rework and keep rounds from dragging.
turns.utterance: Good. I also want each room encounter to end with a clear daily plan and next steps, and the resident can document the daily plan as rounds move along.

turns.inner_thought: As long as those follow-ups are visible on the unit's rounding tracker and reflected where the bedside team looks during the shift, nursing can act on them. If it only lives somewhere the physician team uses, we'll still be chasing updates.
turns.utterance: That should help a lot, as long as action items are tracked where the bedside team can see them and work from them through the rest of the shift.

turns.inner_thought: Residents already document the plan in the note and on their sign-out; I really don't want to introduce another tracker for the pilot. Keeping this in their normal workflow is the only way to get reliable adoption early.
turns.utterance: Yes, and the nice part is that residents already capture the plan in their normal workflow, so I think we can keep that piece pretty lightweight during the pilot.

turns.inner_thought: Okay, I'll have charge nurses treat 8:30 as the time to get the team organized and start pulling nurses in, and they'll keep the unit's action-item workflow current through the morning. That should make this manageable on the floor.
turns.utterance: That works. I'll ask the charge nurses to help pull bedside nurses in once rounds start and to keep the team's action items updated through the morning.

turns.inner_thought: This sounds set: first room at 8:30, resident-managed EHR shared list, narrow hallway exceptions, and plan captured in the resident note/sign-out. That's a clean enough launch plan to start Monday without overcomplicating things.
turns.utterance: Perfect. So it sounds like we're aligned on an 8:30 start, using the shared list before rounds, making bedside rounds the standard except for sensitive patients, and documenting the daily plan during rounds.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I'll brief charge on an 8:30 gathering, the interdisciplinary shared list, broader sensitive-patient flags, and making sure the plan and action items are visible in the unit workflow. From my side, that should have the floor ready.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I'll brief the charge nurses this week so the unit is ready for the Monday rollout.
